stats_pgf_construct.description: Build and read probability generating functions for finite, uniform, binomial, geometric and Poisson random variables.

sections.title: How does one power store one probability?
sections.label: Construct the PGF
sections.intro: Use the value as an exponent and its probability as the coefficient.

blocks.html: \(G_X(t)=\mathrm E(t^X)=\sum_{k\ge0}\mathrm P(X=k)t^k\). The constant is the probability of zero.

figure.alt: Three probability masses at 0, 1 and 3, with no mass at 2.
figure.caption: This discrete law has PGF \(\tfrac12+\tfrac13t+\tfrac16t^3\). The graphical gap at \(2\) gives a missing \(t^2\) term.

blocks.html: The power is the possible value of the random variable. The coefficient is its probability.

blocks.title: Build a four-term PGF
blocks.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\(x\)Probability
\(0\)\(\frac{1}{5}\)
\(1\)\(\frac{2}{5}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{3}{10}\)
\(5\)\(\frac{1}{10}\)

Give the whole generating function, in terms of \(t\).
blocks.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
blocks.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{10} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{10} + \frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{1}{5}\]

blocks.html: Attach each table entry to the correct power. Missing values have coefficient zero.

sections.title: Why does the PGF equal 1 at t = 1?
sections.label: Check the total
sections.intro: Every power of 1 equals 1, including the constant term.

blocks.html: \(G_X(1)=1\) because the probabilities sum to one. Use this condition to find an unknown common multiplier.
Checking the total is necessary, and all individual coefficients also need to be non-negative.

blocks.title: Find a constant and an individual probability
blocks.prompt:
A proposed PGF has the form \(c\left(3 t^{3} + 5 t + 2\right)\).

Find \(c\) and the exact coefficient of \(t^3\).
blocks.hint: The coefficients are non-negative and must add to one.
blocks.solution:
\(G(1)=1\) so \(10c=1\) and \(c=\frac{1}{10}\).

The completed function is \(G_{X}(t)=\frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{t}{2} + \frac{1}{5}\).

blocks.html: Read coefficients after applying the supplied multiplier.

sections.title: How do I build uniform and binomial PGFs?
sections.label: Finite laws
sections.intro: Write one term per possible uniform value. For a binomial count expand a single Bernoulli factor for each trial.

blocks.html: \(G_X(t)=(1-p+pt)^n\) when \(X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\).
A binomial PGF has a term for zero successes even when the smallest positive success count is one.

blocks.title: Generate five equally likely outcomes
blocks.prompt:
\(X\) follows 5 equally likely integer outcomes from 1 to 5.

Give the generating function in terms of \(t\).
blocks.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
blocks.solution:
Write one term per possible result. Every coefficient is \(\frac{1}{5}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{5} + \frac{t^{4}}{5} + \frac{t^{3}}{5} + \frac{t^{2}}{5} + \frac{t}{5}\]

blocks.html: For the uniform model list the actual endpoints before writing the sum.

sections.title: Where does the geometric series start?
sections.label: First success
sections.intro: The geometric variable used here counts the trial of the first success. Its support begins at 1.

blocks.html: \(G_X(t)=\frac{pt}{1-(1-p)t}\) from the geometric series starting with \(pt\).
Omitting the first \(t\) would generate the number of failures before success.

blocks.title: Use the full first-success function
blocks.prompt:
\(X\) follows a geometric distribution with success probability \(\frac{3}{7}\). It counts the trial of the first success.

Give the generating function in terms of \(t\).
blocks.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
blocks.solution:
Factor the first term \(\frac{3 t}{7}\) from the series. The remaining series has common ratio \(\frac{4 t}{7}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3 t}{7 \left(1 - \frac{4 t}{7}\right)}\]

blocks.html: The common ratio is \((1-p)t\).

sections.title: Why does a Poisson PGF use an exponential?
sections.label: Poisson PGF
sections.intro: The factorial denominators match the power series for the exponential function.

blocks.html: \(G_X(t)=\mathrm e^{\lambda(t-1)}\) for \(X\sim\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)\).
Keep the constant multiplier \(\mathrm e^{-\lambda}\). It makes the sum of probabilities equal one.

blocks.title: Read a Poisson probability
blocks.prompt:
\(X\) follows a Poisson distribution with rate \(2\).

Find the probability of exactly 3.
blocks.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
blocks.solution:
Factor \(e^{-2}\) from the power series. The remaining series is the exponential series for \(e^{2 t}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=e^{2 t - 2}\]

Read the coefficient of \(t^{3}\) to get \(\frac{4}{3 e^{2}}\).

blocks.html: The constant coefficient is the probability of zero occurrences.

sections.title: How can a generating function be read backwards?
sections.label: Extract coefficients
sections.intro: Match a desired outcome to its exponent. Expand only as far as needed.

blocks.html: \(\mathrm P(X=k)=[t^k]G_X(t)\). For finite ranges, add the indicated coefficients.
Evaluating \(G_X(k)\) does not extract the probability at \(X=k\).

blocks.title: Read the probability of an absent term
blocks.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3 t^{5}}{8} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{8} + \frac{1}{4}\]

Find the exact probability of \(X=1\).
blocks.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
blocks.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3 t^{5}}{8} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{8} + \frac{1}{4}\]

The coefficient of \(t^{1}\) is \(0\). The constant coefficient is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

blocks.html: If the requested exponent is absent, the probability is zero.

examples.title: Attach each mass to its exponent
examples.question:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\(x\)Probability
\(0\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)
\(1\)\(\frac{1}{3}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{1}{6}\)

Give the whole generating function, in terms of \(t\).
solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{6} + \frac{t}{3} + \frac{1}{2}\]
The possible outcomes are \(0,1,3\), so the coefficient of \(t^2\) is zero. Substitution of \(t=1\) gives \(G_X(1)=1\), confirming the probabilities add to one.

examples.title: Read a missing and a constant probability
examples.question:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{2} + \frac{t}{10} + \frac{2}{5}\]

Find the exact probabilities of \(X=0\) and \(X=2\).
solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{2} + \frac{t}{10} + \frac{2}{5}\]
The coefficient of \(t^{2}\) is \(0\). The constant coefficient is \(\frac{2}{5}\).

examples.title: Find the coefficient multiplier
examples.question:
A proposed PGF has the form \(c\left(6 t^{4} + 3 t + 1\right)\).

Find \(c\) and the exact coefficient of \(t^1\).

examples.title: Form a binomial PGF
examples.question:
\(X\) follows a binomial distribution with 3 trials and success probability \(\frac{1}{3}\).

Give the generating function in terms of \(t\).
solution: One trial has PGF \(\frac{t}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\). The binomial expansion collects the probabilities for all \(3\) independent trials.

examples.title: Start the geometric PGF at the first trial
examples.question:
\(X\) follows a geometric distribution with success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). It counts the trial of the first success.

Give the generating function in terms of \(t\).
solution: Factor the first term \(\frac{2 t}{5}\) from the series. The remaining series has common ratio \(\frac{3 t}{5}\).

examples.title: Recognise the normalised exponential
examples.question:
\(X\) follows a Poisson distribution with rate \(3\).

Give the generating function in terms of \(t\).
solution: Factor \(e^{-3}\) from the power series. The remaining series is the exponential series for \(e^{3 t}\).

examples.title: Read the probability at the fourth power
examples.question:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3 t^{4}}{8} + \frac{t^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{8}\]

Find the exact probability of \(X=4\).
solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3 t^{4}}{8} + \frac{t^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{8}\]
The coefficient of \(t^{4}\) is \(\frac{3}{8}\). The constant coefficient is \(\frac{1}{8}\).

glossary.definition: A power series that stores the probability for each non-negative integer outcome.
The multiplier of a power of \(t\). It gives the probability for the exponent.
The values with positive probability.
The symbol \(t\) labels powers. It is separate from the random variable.

extraPractice.title: Normalise the complete function
extraPractice.prompt:
A proposed PGF has the form \(c\left(3 t^{5} + 4 t^{3} + 2 t^{2} + 3\right)\).

Give the complete normalised PGF.
extraPractice.hint: The coefficients are non-negative and must add to one.

extraPractice.title: Read the mass at the first possible trial
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows a geometric distribution with success probability \(\frac{4}{9}\). It counts the trial of the first success.

Find the smallest possible value of \(X\) and its exact probability.
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
Factor the first term \(\frac{4 t}{9}\) from the series. The remaining series has common ratio \(\frac{5 t}{9}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{4 t}{9 \left(1 - \frac{5 t}{9}\right)}\]

Read the coefficient of \(t^{1}\) to get \(\frac{4}{9}\).

extraPractice.title: Recognise a different rate
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows a Poisson distribution with rate \(4\).

Give the generating function in terms of \(t\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
Factor \(e^{-4}\) from the power series. The remaining series is the exponential series for \(e^{4 t}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=e^{4 t - 4}\]

extraPractice.title: Compute the finite binomial probability
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows a binomial distribution with 4 trials and success probability \(\frac{3}{5}\).

Find the probability of exactly 2.
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
One trial has PGF \(\frac{3 t}{5} + \frac{2}{5}\). The binomial expansion collects the probabilities for all \(4\) independent trials.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{3 t}{5} + \frac{2}{5}\right)^{4}\]

Read the coefficient of \(t^{2}\) to get \(\frac{216}{625}\).

extraPractice.title: Find a later geometric coefficient
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows a geometric distribution with success probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). It counts the trial of the first success.

Find the probability of exactly 4.
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
Factor the first term \(\frac{t}{3}\) from the series. The remaining series has common ratio \(\frac{2 t}{3}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t}{3 \left(1 - \frac{2 t}{3}\right)}\]

Read the coefficient of \(t^{4}\) to get \(\frac{8}{81}\).

extraPractice.title: Read the constant and sixth-power coefficients
extraPractice.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{2 t^{6}}{5} + \frac{3 t^{5}}{10} + \frac{t}{5} + \frac{1}{10}\]

Find the exact probabilities of \(X=0\) and \(X=6\).
extraPractice.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
extraPractice.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{2 t^{6}}{5} + \frac{3 t^{5}}{10} + \frac{t}{5} + \frac{1}{10}\]

The coefficient of \(t^{6}\) is \(\frac{2}{5}\). The constant coefficient is \(\frac{1}{10}\).

stats_pgf_moments.description: Find means, factorial moments and variances from PGFs, and verify them against finite distributions.

sections.title: Why does one derivative give the mean?
sections.label: Mean
sections.intro: Differentiating multiplies every probability by its outcome.

blocks.html: \(\mathrm E(X)=G'_X(1)\). The constant contribution disappears because a zero outcome contributes zero to the mean.
The mean comes from evaluating the derivative at 1. The original function evaluates to 1 for all distributions.

blocks.title: Find a finite mean with gaps
blocks.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{2} + \frac{2 t^{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10}\]

Find the exact mean.
blocks.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
blocks.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{2} + \frac{2 t^{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{5 t^{4}}{2} + \frac{4 t}{5},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=2 \left(5 t^{3} + \frac{2}{5}\right)\]

\(G'_X(1)=\frac{33}{10}\) and \(G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{54}{5}\).

\(\mathrm{Var}(X)=G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)+G_X^\prime(1)-(G_X^\prime(1))^2=\frac{321}{100}\).

blocks.html: Differentiate the entire function first.

sections.title: What does the second derivative actually measure?
sections.label: Factorial moment
sections.intro: The second derivative gives two successive factors from each original exponent.

blocks.html: \(G''_X(1)=\mathrm E[X(X-1)]\). An outcome of zero or one gives no contribution to this expression.
The second factorial moment differs from \(\mathrm E(X^2)\) whenever the mean is nonzero.

blocks.title: Distinguish a factorial moment from a square
blocks.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{5} + \frac{2 t^{3}}{5} + \frac{t}{10} + \frac{3}{10}\]

Find the exact second factorial moment.
blocks.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
blocks.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{5} + \frac{2 t^{3}}{5} + \frac{t}{10} + \frac{3}{10}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{4 t^{3}}{5} + \frac{6 t^{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=\frac{12 t \left(t + 1\right)}{5}\]

\(G'_X(1)=\frac{21}{10}\) and \(G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{24}{5}\).

\(\mathrm{Var}(X)=G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)+G_X^\prime(1)-(G_X^\prime(1))^2=\frac{249}{100}\).

blocks.html: Track the descending factors \(k(k-1)\).

sections.title: How do both derivatives give the variance?
sections.label: Variance
sections.intro: Write \(X^2=X(X-1)+X\) and take expectations.

blocks.html: Square only the mean term, using its unrounded value.

blocks.title: Get variance from four powers
blocks.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{5} + \frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{2 t^{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10}\]

Find the exact variance.
blocks.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
blocks.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{5} + \frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{2 t^{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{6 t^{5}}{5} + \frac{9 t^{2}}{10} + \frac{4 t}{5},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=6 t^{4} + \frac{9 t}{5} + \frac{4}{5}\]

\(G'_X(1)=\frac{29}{10}\) and \(G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{43}{5}\).

\(\mathrm{Var}(X)=G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)+G_X^\prime(1)-(G_X^\prime(1))^2=\frac{309}{100}\).

blocks.html: A negative variance signals an arithmetic error.

sections.title: Can a factored form simplify derivatives?
sections.label: Factored PGFs
sections.intro: A compact binomial or power form often makes the chain rule faster than expanding.

blocks.html: Find \(G'_X(t)\) and \(G''_X(t)\) before substituting \(t=1\). A term like \((a+bt)^n\) produces a factor \(b\) at each differentiation.
The multiplier from the inner function is needed at each use of the chain rule.

blocks.title: Chain rule with the common probability
blocks.prompt:
\(X\) follows a binomial distribution with 5 trials and success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\).

Find the exact mean and variance.
blocks.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
blocks.solution:
One trial has PGF \(\frac{t}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\). The binomial expansion collects the probabilities for all \(5\) independent trials.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{t}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\right)^{5}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{5 \left(t + 3\right)^{4}}{1024},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=\frac{5 \left(t + 3\right)^{3}}{256}\]

\(G_X^\prime(1)=\frac{5}{4},\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{5}{4},\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{15}{16}\).

blocks.html: Note where the inside expression equals one.

sections.title: How do I handle an infinite distribution?
sections.label: Geometric moments
sections.intro: A convergent rational PGF is often simpler to differentiate than the whole series.

blocks.html: Rewrite the denominator as a negative power or use the quotient rule. For a geometric first-success count the variance is \(\tfrac{1-p}{p^2}\).
Substituting one into an undifferentiated PGF gives the total probability, regardless of how many outcomes it has.

blocks.title: Find the moments of a first-success count
blocks.prompt:
\(X\) follows a geometric distribution with success probability \(\frac{5}{8}\). It counts the trial of the first success.

Find the exact mean and variance.
blocks.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
blocks.solution:
Factor the first term \(\frac{5 t}{8}\) from the series. The remaining series has common ratio \(\frac{3 t}{8}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{5 t}{8 \left(1 - \frac{3 t}{8}\right)}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{40}{\left(3 t - 8\right)^{2}},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=- \frac{240}{\left(3 t - 8\right)^{3}}\]

\(G_X^\prime(1)=\frac{8}{5},\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{48}{25},\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{24}{25}\).

blocks.html: Check that the function is defined in a neighbourhood of 1.

sections.title: How can the distribution check my answer?
sections.label: Cross-check
sections.intro: For finite laws the original coefficients allow a second method.

blocks.html: \(\sum_k kp_k\) gives the mean and \(\sum_k(k-\mu)^2p_k\) gives the variance. Compare with the derivatives.
If a PGF is expanded to check moments, keep the zero and missing powers straight.

blocks.title: Use both exact moments from a table
blocks.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\(x\)Probability
\(0\)\(\frac{2}{5}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{1}{5}\)
\(5\)\(\frac{3}{10}\)
\(6\)\(\frac{1}{10}\)

Find the exact mean and variance.
blocks.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
blocks.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{10} + \frac{3 t^{5}}{10} + \frac{t^{2}}{5} + \frac{2}{5}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{3 t^{5}}{5} + \frac{3 t^{4}}{2} + \frac{2 t}{5},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=3 t^{4} + 6 t^{3} + \frac{2}{5}\]

\(G'_X(1)=\frac{5}{2}\) and \(G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{47}{5}\).

\(\mathrm{Var}(X)=G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)+G_X^\prime(1)-(G_X^\prime(1))^2=\frac{113}{20}\).

blocks.html: An exact rational calculation avoids cumulative rounding.

glossary.definition: At \(t=1\), it yields the expected count.
\(\mathrm E[X(X-1)]\), the value of the second derivative at 1.
\(\mathrm E(X^2)\) combines the two derivatives evaluated at 1.
The second ordinary moment minus the square of the mean.

extraPractice.title: Combine mean and variance as exact fractions
extraPractice.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{10} + \frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{t}{5} + \frac{2}{5}\]

Find the exact mean and variance.
extraPractice.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
extraPractice.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{10} + \frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{t}{5} + \frac{2}{5}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{3 t^{5}}{5} + \frac{9 t^{2}}{10} + \frac{1}{5},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=3 t \left(t^{3} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\]

\(G'_X(1)=\frac{17}{10}\) and \(G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{24}{5}\).

\(\mathrm{Var}(X)=G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)+G_X^\prime(1)-(G_X^\prime(1))^2=\frac{361}{100}\).

extraPractice.title: Recognise equal Poisson mean and variance
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows a Poisson distribution with rate \(5\).

Find the exact mean and variance.
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
Factor \(e^{-5}\) from the power series. The remaining series is the exponential series for \(e^{5 t}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=e^{5 t - 5}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{5 e^{5 t}}{e^{5}},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=\frac{25 e^{5 t}}{e^{5}}\]

\(G_X^\prime(1)=5,\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=25,\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=5\).

extraPractice.title: Find the factorial moment of a binomial count
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows a binomial distribution with 5 trials and success probability \(\frac{4}{7}\).

Find the exact second factorial moment.
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
One trial has PGF \(\frac{4 t}{7} + \frac{3}{7}\). The binomial expansion collects the probabilities for all \(5\) independent trials.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{4 t}{7} + \frac{3}{7}\right)^{5}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{20 \left(4 t + 3\right)^{4}}{16807},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=\frac{320 \left(4 t + 3\right)^{3}}{16807}\]

\(G_X^\prime(1)=\frac{20}{7},\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{320}{49},\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{60}{49}\).

extraPractice.title: Use a geometric factorial moment
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows a geometric distribution with success probability \(\frac{2}{7}\). It counts the trial of the first success.

Find the exact second factorial moment.
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
Factor the first term \(\frac{2 t}{7}\) from the series. The remaining series has common ratio \(\frac{5 t}{7}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{2 t}{7 \left(1 - \frac{5 t}{7}\right)}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{14}{\left(5 t - 7\right)^{2}},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=- \frac{140}{\left(5 t - 7\right)^{3}}\]

\(G_X^\prime(1)=\frac{7}{2},\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{35}{2},\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{35}{4}\).

extraPractice.title: Find both moments of the discrete uniform law
extraPractice.prompt:
\(X\) follows 6 equally likely integer outcomes from 1 to 6.

Find the exact mean and variance.
extraPractice.hint: Write the possible values down first. Then use the probability for each exponent.
extraPractice.solution:
Write one term per possible result. Every coefficient is \(\frac{1}{6}\).

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{6} + \frac{t^{5}}{6} + \frac{t^{4}}{6} + \frac{t^{3}}{6} + \frac{t^{2}}{6} + \frac{t}{6}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{6 t^{5} + 5 t^{4} + 4 t^{3} + 3 t^{2} + 2 t + 1}{6},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=\frac{15 t^{4} + 10 t^{3} + 6 t^{2} + 3 t + 1}{3}\]

\(G_X^\prime(1)=\frac{7}{2},\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{35}{3},\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{35}{12}\).

extraPractice.title: Confirm the variance when zero has positive mass
extraPractice.prompt:
A scoring device returns a non-negative integer count.

\(x\)Probability
\(0\)\(\frac{3}{5}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{3}{10}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{1}{10}\)

Find the exact variance.
extraPractice.hint: The coefficient gives the probability for that exponent. For moments, differentiate before substituting 1.
extraPractice.solution:
Attach the probability to the power for its value.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{10} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{10} + \frac{3}{5}\]\[G_X^\prime(t)=\frac{2 t^{3}}{5} + \frac{3 t}{5},\qquad G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=\frac{3 \left(2 t^{2} + 1\right)}{5}\]

\(G'_X(1)=1\) and \(G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=\frac{9}{5}\).

\(\mathrm{Var}(X)=G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)+G_X^\prime(1)-(G_X^\prime(1))^2=\frac{9}{5}\).

stats_pgf_transform.description: Shift and scale integer outcomes in a PGF, and find sum probabilities from a joint distribution when counts are dependent.

sections.title: Why does a shift multiply by a power?
sections.label: Shift
sections.intro: Adding a fixed integer to every value raises every exponent by that integer.

blocks.html: \(G_{X+b}(t)=t^bG_X(t)\) for a non-negative shift \(b\).
It shifts all powers, including an original constant term.

blocks.title: Report a complete shifted PGF
blocks.prompt:
A count \(X\) has PGF \(G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{2} + \frac{t}{5} + \frac{3}{10}\). Define \(Y=X + 2\).

Give the generating function for \(Y\).
blocks.hint: A shift multiplies by a power of t. A scale changes the power inside the original function.
blocks.solution:
\(t^Y=t^{2}(t^{1})^X\).

\[G_{Y}(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{2} + \frac{t^{3}}{5} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{10}\]

The transformed mean and variance are \(\frac{37}{10}\) and \(\frac{181}{100}\).

blocks.html: A shift makes the lowest possible value larger by exactly the same amount.

sections.title: Why does a scale replace t by a power?
sections.label: Scale
sections.intro: Doubling a count doubles every outcome exponent.

blocks.html: \(G_{aX}(t)=G_X(t^a)\) for positive integer \(a\).
Changing the multiplier of every term would change probabilities, and their total would no longer equal one.

blocks.title: Find a power removed by scaling
blocks.prompt:
A count \(X\) has PGF \(G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{2} + \frac{3 t}{10} + \frac{1}{5}\). Define \(Y=3 X\).

Find the exact probability that the transformed value is 5.
blocks.hint: A shift multiplies by a power of t. A scale changes the power inside the original function.
blocks.solution:
\(t^Y=t^{0}(t^{3})^X\).

\[G_{Y}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{2} + \frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{1}{5}\]

The transformed mean and variance are \(\frac{39}{10}\) and \(\frac{549}{100}\).

blocks.html: A power that cannot appear by scaling has zero probability.

sections.title: How do I combine a shift and a scale?
sections.label: Both operations
sections.intro: Apply the exponent identity to the whole value.

blocks.html: \(G_{aX+b}(t)=t^bG_X(t^a)\) follows by writing \(t^{aX+b}=t^b(t^a)^X\).
When calculating variance the shift contributes zero and the scale is squared.

A count \(X\) has PGF \(G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{5} + \frac{t}{2} + \frac{3}{10}\). Define \(Y=2 X + 2\).

Find the exact probability that the transformed value is 4.
blocks.hint: A shift multiplies by a power of t. A scale changes the power inside the original function.
blocks.solution:
\(t^Y=t^{2}(t^{2})^X\).

\[G_{Y}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{5} + \frac{t^{4}}{2} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{10}\]

The transformed mean and variance are \(\frac{19}{5}\) and \(\frac{49}{25}\).

blocks.html: Read the transformed support before extracting a coefficient.

sections.title: How do the margins test independence?
sections.label: Joint laws
sections.intro: Sum the cells in each row and column to obtain the individual masses.

blocks.html: Independence requires \(\mathrm P(X=i,Y=j)=\mathrm P(X=i)\mathrm P(Y=j)\) for every pair.
One pair that matches the product does not establish independence.

blocks.title: Detect a failure of marginal factorisation
blocks.prompt:
A joint distribution for two counts is given.

Joint probability\(Y=0\)\(Y=1\)
\(X=0\)\(\frac{5}{12}\)\(\frac{1}{12}\)
\(X=1\)\(\frac{1}{12}\)\(\frac{5}{12}\)

Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent?
blocks.hint: For a sum, add the joint probabilities on the diagonal with the required total.
blocks.solution:
For example, \(\mathrm P(X=0,Y=0)=\frac{5}{12}\) and the product of the marginals is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

The sum's coefficient is \(\sum_{i+j=1}\mathrm P(X=i,Y=j)\) for exponent \(1\), giving \(\frac{1}{6}\).

\[G_{X+Y}(t)=\frac{5 t^{2}}{12} + \frac{t}{6} + \frac{5}{12}\]

blocks.html: One counterexample is sufficient to show dependence.

sections.title: How do I find a sum when the counts depend on each other?
sections.label: Add joint masses
sections.intro: The sum event collects all cells on the relevant diagonal.

blocks.html: \(\mathrm P(X+Y=k)=\sum_{i+j=k}\mathrm P(X=i,Y=j)\). Use the actual joint values.
Replacing the listed joint probabilities with products of margins silently assumes independence.

Joint probability\(Y=0\)\(Y=1\)\(Y=2\)

\(X=1\)\(\frac{1}{20}\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{10}\)
\(X=2\)\(\frac{1}{10}\)\(\frac{1}{10}\)\(\frac{1}{20}\)

Find the exact probability of a sum of 2.
blocks.hint: For a sum, add the joint probabilities on the diagonal with the required total.
blocks.solution:
For example, \(\mathrm P(X=0,Y=0)=\frac{1}{10}\) and the product of the marginals is \(\frac{7}{80}\).

The sum's coefficient is \(\sum_{i+j=2}\mathrm P(X=i,Y=j)\) for exponent \(2\), giving \(\frac{11}{20}\).

\[G_{X+Y}(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{20} + \frac{t^{3}}{5} + \frac{11 t^{2}}{20} + \frac{t}{10} + \frac{1}{10}\]

\[G_S(t)=t^{1}G_X(t^{2})G_Y(t)=\frac{3 t^{5}}{50} + \frac{2 t^{4}}{25} + \frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{8 t^{2}}{25} + \frac{6 t}{25}\]

stats_pgf_copies.description: Raise a PGF to a power for repeated independent copies, and find support, exact total probabilities and moments.

sections.title: Why is a repeated sum a power?
sections.label: Repeated sum
sections.intro: Each observation contributes a factor and every factor has the same form.

blocks.html: \(G_{X_1+\cdots+X_n}(t)=[G_X(t)]^n\) for independent identically distributed copies.
The exponent is the number of independent copies. Multiplying the single-copy PGF by this number would break normalisation.

blocks.title: Build the PGF of three plays
blocks.prompt:
A points game is played 3 times independently with the same single-play law.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{3} + \frac{t}{6} + \frac{1}{2}\]

Let \(T\) be the total.

Give the full PGF for the total.
blocks.hint: Raise the single-play PGF to the number of plays, then read the required coefficient or moment.
blocks.solution:
\(G_T(t)=[G_X(t)]^{3}\) because there is an independent factor for each play.

\[G_{T}(t)=\frac{t^{6}}{27} + \frac{t^{5}}{18} + \frac{7 t^{4}}{36} + \frac{37 t^{3}}{216} + \frac{7 t^{2}}{24} + \frac{t}{8} + \frac{1}{8}\]

blocks.html: Write one factor for each observation you actually sum.

sections.title: What are the smallest and largest totals?
sections.label: Support
sections.intro: If the single-copy minimum and maximum are finite, add them over all copies.

blocks.html: \(\min S=n\min X,\quad \max S=n\max X\) because those extreme choices can occur together.
A total inside the endpoints can still be impossible if the support has gaps.

blocks.title: Find the limits for shifted positive scores
blocks.prompt:

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{2} + \frac{3 t^{3}}{10} + \frac{t^{2}}{5}\]

Let \(T\) be the total.

Give the smallest and largest possible totals.
blocks.hint: Raise the single-play PGF to the number of plays, then read the required coefficient or moment.
blocks.solution:
\(G_T(t)=[G_X(t)]^{3}\) because there is an independent factor for each play.

\[G_{T}(t)=\frac{t^{12}}{8} + \frac{9 t^{11}}{40} + \frac{57 t^{10}}{200} + \frac{207 t^{9}}{1000} + \frac{57 t^{8}}{500} + \frac{9 t^{7}}{250} + \frac{t^{6}}{125}\]

The lowest and highest powers give \(6\) and \(12\).

blocks.html: A fixed smallest value above zero shifts the entire repeated sum.

sections.title: How many patterns make a particular total?
sections.label: Single probability
sections.intro: Factor the polynomial first and identify the target coefficient.

blocks.html: Different orders of the same outcomes can contribute separately. For exactly one nonzero observation, choose which copy supplies it.
Using a single ordering undercounts when the nonzero score could come from several copies.

blocks.title: Find the probability of a total of one
blocks.prompt:
A points game is played 4 times independently with the same single-play law.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3 t^{2}}{10} + \frac{3 t}{10} + \frac{2}{5}\]

Let \(T\) be the total.

Find the exact probability of a total of 1.
blocks.hint: Raise the single-play PGF to the number of plays, then read the required coefficient or moment.
blocks.solution:
\(G_T(t)=[G_X(t)]^{4}\) because there is an independent factor for each play.

\[G_{T}(t)=\frac{81 t^{8}}{10000} + \frac{81 t^{7}}{2500} + \frac{459 t^{6}}{5000} + \frac{81 t^{5}}{500} + \frac{2241 t^{4}}{10000} + \frac{27 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{102 t^{2}}{625} + \frac{48 t}{625} + \frac{16}{625}\]
Unordered patternOrdersProbability over these orders
\(\left(0,0,0,1\right)\)\(4\)\(\frac{48}{625}\)

Add the pattern contributions to obtain \(\frac{48}{625}\).

blocks.html: If using an expansion, include all terms that reach the target exponent.

sections.title: Can I work out moments before expanding?
sections.label: Efficient moments
sections.intro: For independent copies each occurrence contributes the same mean and variance.

blocks.html: \(\mathrm E(S)=n\mathrm E(X),\quad \mathrm{Var}(S)=n\mathrm{Var}(X)\).
Multiplying a random variable by \(n\) has variance factor \(n^2\). Summing \(n\) independent copies has variance factor \(n\).

blocks.title: Find the mean and variance after four plays
blocks.prompt:
A points game is played 4 times independently with the same single-play law.

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{10} + \frac{3 t}{10} + \frac{3}{5}\]

Let \(T\) be the total.

Give the exact mean and variance of the total.
blocks.hint: Raise the single-play PGF to the number of plays, then read the required coefficient or moment.
blocks.solution:
\(G_T(t)=[G_X(t)]^{4}\) because there is an independent factor for each play.

\[G_{T}(t)=\frac{t^{8}}{10000} + \frac{3 t^{7}}{2500} + \frac{39 t^{6}}{5000} + \frac{81 t^{5}}{2500} + \frac{189 t^{4}}{2000} + \frac{243 t^{3}}{1250} + \frac{351 t^{2}}{1250} + \frac{162 t}{625} + \frac{81}{625}\]

The single-play mean and variance are \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{9}{20}\). The total has mean \(2\) and variance \(\frac{9}{5}\).

blocks.html: The standard deviation of the total is \(\sqrt n\) times the single-copy standard deviation.

sections.title: Can a repeated total be recognised immediately?
sections.label: Recognise the law
sections.intro: Repeated Poisson counts and repeated binomial counts with the same success probability give familiar PGFs.

blocks.html: A power multiplies the Poisson rate or the binomial trial count. In a binomial model the success probability per trial stays the same.
Don’t change the binomial success probability by raising it to the number of repeats.

blocks.title: Recognise two identical binomial counts
blocks.prompt:
The counts are independent. Their laws are \(X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(3,\frac{2}{5}),\quad Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(3,\frac{2}{5})\).

Identify the distribution of the sum.
blocks.hint: Multiply PGFs and combine identical bases or exponential powers.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the two PGFs.

\[G_{X+Y}(t)=\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)^{6}\]

Recognise this as \(\mathrm{Bin}(6,\frac{2}{5})\).

blocks.html: Check familiarity only after confirming the model form.

sections.title: How can I distinguish repeated copies from a scaled single copy?
sections.label: Choose the operation
sections.intro: Repeated copies allow different outcomes. A scaled copy takes one value and repeats that value by multiplication.

blocks.html: \(G_{X_1+\cdots+X_n}(t)=[G_X(t)]^n\) whereas \(G_{nX}(t)=G_X(t^n)\).
The means agree. The variance and support can distinguish the two distributions.
